# Chapter 7: Exceptions

Rules that no analyzer enforces (judgment), and CONSIDER rules that analyzers only suggest. Open the examples file for the explanation and code the book gives with each rule.

## 7.1 Exception Throwing

- **FDG7001** DO NOT return error codes. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7001
- **FDG7002** DO report execution failures by throwing exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7002
- **FDG7003** CONSIDER terminating the process by calling `System.Environment.FailFast` instead of throwing an exception if your code encounters a situation where immediate process termination is necessary. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7003
- **FDG7004** DO NOT use exceptions for the normal flow of control, if possible. Prefer Tester–Doer or the Try pattern to throwing exceptions in common cases. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7004
- **FDG7005** CONSIDER the performance implications of throwing exceptions. Throw rates greater than 100 per second are likely to noticeably impact the performance of most applications. See section 7.5 for details.
- **FDG7006** DO document all exceptions thrown by publicly callable members because of a violation of the member contract (rather than a system failure) and treat them as part of your contract. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7006
- **FDG7009** CONSIDER using exception builder methods. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7009

## 7.2 Choosing the Right Type of Exception to Throw

- **FDG7012** DO NOT create new exception types to communicate usage errors. Throw one of the existing base library exceptions instead. See section 7.3 for detailed usage guidelines for the most common standard exception types. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7012
- **FDG7013** CONSIDER creating and throwing custom exceptions if you have a program error condition that can be programmatically handled in a different way than any other existing exception. Otherwise, throw one of the existing exceptions. See section 7.4 for details on creating custom exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7013
- **FDG7014** DO NOT create a new exception type if the exception would not be handled differently than an existing framework exception. Throw the existing framework exception in such case. See section 7.3 for detailed usage guidelines for the most common standard exception types. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7014
- **FDG7015** DO create a new exception type to communicate a unique program error that cannot be communicated using an existing framework exception. See section 7.4 for details on creating custom exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7015
- **FDG7016** AVOID creating APIs that when called can result in a system failure. If such a failure can occur, call `Environment.FailFast` instead of throwing an exception when the system failure occurs. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7016
- **FDG7017** DO NOT create and throw new exceptions just to have your feature name in the exception type or namespace name.

## 7.2.1 Error Message Design

- **FDG7020** DO ensure that exception messages are grammatically correct. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7020
- **FDG7023** DO NOT disclose security-sensitive information in exception messages.
- **FDG7024** CONSIDER localizing the exception messages thrown by your components if you expect your components to be used by developers speaking different languages. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7024

## 7.2.2 Exception Handling

- **FDG7027** DO NOT exclude any special exceptions when catching for the purpose of transferring exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7027
- **FDG7028** CONSIDER catching a specific exception when you understand why it was thrown in a given context and can respond to the failure programmatically. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7028
- **FDG7029** DO NOT overcatch. Exceptions should often be allowed to propagate up the call stack. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7029
- **FDG7030** DO use try-finally and avoid using try-catch for cleanup code. In well-written exception code, try-finally is far more common than try-catch. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7030
- **FDG7032** DO use `ExceptionDispatchInfo` when rethrowing an exception from a different context. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7032

## 7.2.3 Wrapping Exceptions

- **FDG7034** CONSIDER wrapping specific exceptions thrown from a lower layer in a more appropriate exception if the lower layer is just an implementation detail for the operation. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7034
- **FDG7035** AVOID catching and wrapping nonspecific exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7035

## 7.3.3 InvalidOperationException

- **FDG7041** DO throw an `InvalidOperationException` if the object is in an inappropriate state. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7041

## 7.3.4 ArgumentException, ArgumentNullException, and ArgumentOutOfRangeException

- **FDG7042** DO throw `ArgumentException` or one of its subtypes if bad arguments are passed to a member. Prefer the most derived exception type, if applicable.

## 7.3.9 OperationCanceledException and TaskCanceledException

- **FDG7050** DO throw `OperationCanceledException` to represent any caller-initiated abort or cancellation.

## 7.3.10 FormatException

- **FDG7052** DO throw `FormatException` to indicate the input string in a text parsing method does not conform to the required, or specified, format.
- **FDG7053** DO throw `FormatException` to indicate the format specifier string to a text parsing or text formatting method is invalid. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7053

## 7.3.11 PlatformNotSupportedException

- **FDG7054** DO throw `PlatformNotSupportedException` to indicate the operation cannot complete in the current runtime environment but could on a different runtime or operating system. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7054

## 7.4 Designing Custom Exceptions

- **FDG7055** DO derive exceptions from `System.Exception` or one of the other common base exceptions.
- **FDG7056** AVOID deep exception hierarchies. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7056
- **FDG7060** CONSIDER providing exception properties for programmatic access to extra information (besides the message string) relevant to the exception.

## 7.5 Exceptions and Performance

- **FDG7061** DO NOT use error codes because of concerns that exceptions might affect performance negatively. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7061

## 7.5.1 The Tester–Doer Pattern

- **FDG7062** CONSIDER the Tester–Doer Pattern for members that might throw exceptions in common scenarios to avoid performance problems related to exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7062

## 7.5.2 The Try Pattern

- **FDG7063** CONSIDER the Try Pattern for members that might throw exceptions in common scenarios to avoid performance problems related to exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7063
- **FDG7065** DO pick one kind of reason for why your Try method can return `false`, and throw an exception for any other failure reason. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7065
- **FDG7066** DO provide an exception-throwing member for each member using the Try Pattern. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7066

## 7.5.2.1 Value-Producing Try Methods

- **FDG7067** DO “return” the value from a Try method via an `out` parameter. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7067
- **FDG7068** DO write `default(T)` to the `out` parameter from a Try method that returns `false`. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7068
- **FDG7069** AVOID writing to the `out` parameter from a Try method when throwing an exception. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7069

## 7.5.2.1 Static TryParse(string, out T) Methods

- **FDG7070** DO return `false` on null inputs to a method of the form `static bool TryParse(string, out T value)`. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions.md#fdg7070
